title: Distance Approximating Minors for Planar and Minor-Free Graphs
authors: Hsien-Chih Chang (Dartmouth College, USA), Jonathan Conroy (Dartmouth College, USA)
abstract: Given an edge-weighted graph $G$ and a subset of vertices $T$ called terminals, an $\alpha$-distance-approximating minor ($\alpha$-DAM) of $G$ is a graph minor $H$ of $G$ that contains all terminals, such that the distance between every pair of terminals is preserved up to a factor of $\alpha$. Distance-approximating minor would be an effective distance-sketching structure on minor-closed family of graphs; in the constant-stretch regime it generalizes the well-known Steiner Point Removal problem by allowing the existence of (a small number of) non-terminal vertices. Unfortunately, in the $(1+\varepsilon)$ regime the only known DAM construction for planar graphs relies on overlaying $\tilde{O}_\varepsilon(|T|)$ shortest paths in $G$, which naturally leads to a quadratic bound in the number of terminals [Cheung, Goranci, and Henzinger, ICALP 2016]. We break the quadratic barrier and build the first $(1+\varepsilon)$-distance-approximating minor for k-terminal planar graphs and minor-free graphs of near-linear size $\tilde{O}_\varepsilon(k)$. In addition to the near-optimality in size, the construction relies only on the existence of shortest-path separators [Abraham and Gavoille, PODC 2006] and $\varepsilon$-covers [Thorup, J. ACM 2004]. Consequently, this provides an alternative and simpler construction to the near-linear-size emulator for planar graphs [Chang, Krauthgamer, and Tan, STOC 2022], as well as the first near-linear-size emulator for minor-free graphs. Our DAM can be constructed in near-linear time.

Abstract—Given an edge-weighted graph G and a subset of
vertices T called terminals, an α-distance-approximating minor
(α-DAM) of G is a graph minor H of G that contains all
terminals, such that the distance between every pair of terminals is preserved up to a factor of α. Distance-approximating
minor would be an effective distance-sketching structure on
minor-closed family of graphs; in the constant-stretch regime
it generalizes the well-known Steiner Point Removal problem
by allowing the existence of (a small number of) non-terminal
vertices. Unfortunately, in the (1 + ε) regime the only known
DAM construction for planar graphs relies on overlaying Õε (|T |)
shortest paths in G, which naturally leads to a quadratic bound
in the number of terminals [Cheung, Goranci, and Henzinger,
ICALP 2016].
We break the quadratic barrier and build the first (1 + ε)distance-approximating minor for k-terminal planar graphs and
minor-free graphs of near-linear size Õε (k). In addition to
the near-optimality in size, the construction relies only on the
existence of shortest-path separators [Abraham and Gavoille,
PODC 2006] and ε-covers [Thorup, J. ACM 2004]. Consequently,
this provides an alternative and simpler construction to the nearlinear-size emulator for planar graphs [Chang, Krauthgamer, and
Tan, STOC 2022], as well as the first near-linear-size emulator for
minor-free graphs. Our DAM can be constructed in near-linear
time.

A recent breakthrough result by Chang, Krauthgamer, and

They performed a split-and-combine strategy by cutting and

be achieved in planar graphs), and then proceed to identify a
carefully chosen shortest-path separator that splits the piece in
a (roughly) balanced fashion and compute ε-cover on the path

very delicate and crucially relies on the piece being planar
with exactly one boundary to work. As a result, there is no

graphs (or even for apex-minor-free graphs).

I. I NTRODUCTION
Distance compression and sketching have proven to be
ubiquitous in modern graph algorithm design. In this paper
we study a natural distance sketching structure on planar and
minor-free graphs whose existence is unknown but has been
alluded to, with algorithmic consequences [1], [2]. Let G be
an undirected edge-weighted graph from some minor-closed
family. Our goal is to preserve pairwise distances between a
subset of vertices in G called terminals; we denote the set
of terminals as T . A stretch-α distance-approximating minor
of G (shorthanded as α-DAM) [3], [4] is an (edge-weighted1 )
graph minor H of G that contains all terminals in T as vertices
and possibly other vertices in G, such that for every pair of
terminals x and y,
dG (x, y) ≤ dH (x, y) ≤ α · dG (x, y).
Distance-approximating minors generalize the well-studied
notion of spanners, which are required to be subgraphs of
G. Generally speaking, spanners cannot have size depending
only on the terminal set (for example, think of a single path
with only the two endpoints as terminals) and are usually
measured in terms of lightness (the ratio of its weight to that
of the minimum spanning tree). Therefore spanners are useful
for applications related to connectivity problems like Steiner
tree and TSP [5], [6], but unable to help with distance-related
optimization tasks like distance oracles or (approximate) diameter. On the other hand, distance-approximating minors retain
the structure of the input graph G compared to more relaxed
distance sketching structures like emulators, where the vertices
and edges can come from out of nowhere (unrelated to G) as
long as the terminals in T are still present and their distances
are preserved pairwise. Emulators can be useful for distance
inquiries on planar graphs (after submitting to the standard
graph decomposition pipeline using r-division [7], [8]), but
fall short in their ability to return an actual path realizing the
approximate distance.
Constructing distance-approximating minors has proven to
be difficult, even for popular minor-closed families like planar
graphs. It is straightforward to construct (exact) DAM in
any graph with O(|T |4 ) vertices by overlaying the (unique)
shortest path between every pair of terminals in G [3]; however
it is impossible to construct an exact DAM with subquadratic
size [3], [9], even when the input graph is a planar grid. At the
other extreme, if we restrict the size of the DAM to be exactly
|T |, forbidding any non-terminal vertex to occur in H, then
this is the famous Steiner Point Removal problem [10]–[17],
where the lower bound on stretch is at least 8(1 − o(1)) [18]
when the graph is minor-free, and getting O(1)-stretch was an
open problem for two decades until recently being resolved by
Chang, Conroy, Le, Milenković, Solomon, and Than [19]–[21]
on planar and minor-free graphs.

Our result gives the first ever construction for (1 + ε)DAM on planar graphs, as well as on minor-free graphs,
that has size near-linear in |T |. From a technical point of
view, our strategy is (perhaps surprisingly) a refinement of
the shortest-path overlay approach. Our construction bypasses
the need for a planar embedding and directly works with
shortest-path separators and ε-covers; not only does this makes
the construction generalizable to minor-free graphs, but also
provides a new alternative construction to the (1+ε)-emulator
for planar graphs that are cleaner both in description and
in proofs. (The CKT construction spans 50 pages and is
quite delicate.) To avoid the quadratic blowup from overlaying
shortest paths, we carefully detour the paths to construct a set
of approximate shortest paths that (in some amortized sense)
intersect sparsely with each other. We believe this technique
may be of independent interest.
Remark 1.2. One drawback of our Theorem 1.1 is that the size
of DAM has a poly log dependence on the graph size n and the
maximum edge weight Φ, whereas previous results (namely, the
DAMs of [3] and [4], and the emulator of [2]) depend only on
the number of terminals |T |. We could remove the dependence
on n by first computing the exact O(|T |4 )-size DAM of [3]
and then applying our DAM on top of the O(|T |4 )-size graph,
but it is unclear how to remove the dependence on Φ. These
extra dependencies don’t bother much for our applications, but
it would be interesting to construct a DAM without dependence
on Φ.
a) Applications: In minor-free graphs, DAM is particularly helpful because it enables efficient distance compression
on regions of an r-division of the input graph and can thus

running time so far remains quadratic [23], [26]. (We did not
improve the construction time for path separators; it remains
to be an interesting open question.)

B. Technical Overview
Let G be a connected n-vertex planar graph with diameter

in any n-vertex planar graph, there is a set of O(1) shortest

(which we often call regions) each with at most 2n/3 vertices.

Recursively applying the shortest-path separator theorem on
the resulting pieces yields a separator hierarchy: a hierarchical
partition of the graph into regions. For each region R in the
separator hierarchy, the internal separator is a set of O(1)
paths whose removal splits R into roughly equal-sized pieces;
the external separators are the set of O(log n) paths which
are the internal separators of all ancestor pieces of R. Note
that any path in G that starts inside region R and then leaves
R must pass through some external separator of R.
Along each separator path we place portals, as in [22]. For
each region R, and each internal separator path P for region
R, we define the scale-i portals to be a minimal set of vertices
on P such that every vertex of P is within distance ≤ ε2i of
some scale-i portal.4 Notice that for every vertex v ∈ R, there
are only O(ε−1 ) scale-i portals on P that are within distance
O(2i ) of v. If p is a scale-i portal within distance O(2i ) of
vertex v, we say that p is a relevant portal for v. Intuitively, the
relevant portals of v are enough to capture (1+ε)-approximate
distances between v and any vertex on P .5 We construct our
non-planar (1+ε)-distortion emulator H similarly to the +εD
case:
Initialize H as an empty graph with vertex set V (G).
For every region R in the separator hierarchy, and for
every terminal t in R: add (to H) an edge between
t and every relevant portal of t on the internal
separator paths of R.
The size of H is O(|T |ε−1 log2 n): every terminal is contained
in O(log n) regions, each of which contains O(ε−1 log n)
relevant portals. Moreover, one can show that H preserves
distances up to a 1 + ε multiplicative factor. Indeed, let t1 and
t2 be two terminals. Let π be the shortest path in G between
t1 and t2 , let i be the smallest scale with δG (t1 , t2 ) ≤ 2i ,
and let R be the lowest region that contains both t1 and t2 .
Any path between t1 and t2 must pass through an internal or
external separator of R; in particular, π passes through an
internal separator of some region R′ which is an ancestor

scale-i portal p (relevant to both t1 and t2 ) on an internal
separator of R′ such that p is within distance ε · 2i of π.
Triangle inequality implies that, in the emulator H, the edges
(t1 , p) and (p, t2 ) form a 2-hop path with length at most
δG (t1 , t2 ) + 2ε · 2i = (1 + O(ε)) · δG (t1 , t2 ).

Let’s try to generalize this +εD DAM construction to (1 + ε)

of scale-i portals (p, p′ ), where p is a scale-i portal on an
internal separator of R, p′ is a scale-i portal on an internal

Initialize H as an empty graph with vertex set
V (G). Let R be the set of regions in the separator
hierarchy which contain some terminal. For every
region R ∈ R, for every canonical pair (p, p′ ) of
R which is relevant to some terminal t in R: add
(to H) a shortest path in R between p and p′ . After

The resulting DAM has small distortion — one can argue that
the relevant canonical pairs are enough to preserve distances
between terminals: this is formalized in Lemma 3.2 (the

“Relevant Pairs Lemma”) and Section V. Unfortunately, the
DAM may be too large: it could be as large as Õε (|T |2 ).
Before explaining how to resolve the issue, we discuss why
the DAM could be large, i.e., how a large number of splitting
points could arise. As in the +εD case, we imagine processing
the regions in root-to-leaf order. When we process each region
R, imagine drawing the paths between canonical pairs in
order from longest to shortest. Now consider an arbitrary
path π added between some scale-i canonical pair when we
process region R. One can show that, when path π is added,
it intersects only Õε (1) other paths that are longer than π.
(Intuitively, π can’t be close to too many portals at scale ≥ i;
this follows from the fact that separator paths are shortest
paths.) One might hope that this is enough for some charging
argument to bound the size of H. However, π could intersect
an unbounded number of paths shorter than π; although we
add paths from longest-to-shortest within region R, we may
have added many short paths to our DAM already when an
ancestor region of R was processed. See Figure 2 for an
example.
d) The key idea — detour paths: Instead of adding the
shortest path between a canonical pair of portals, we add
an approximate shortest path that intersects only Õε (1) paths
added earlier. Let (p, p′ ) be a canonical pair in region R, and
initialize π to be the shortest path between p and p′ in R.
As discussed above, π can only intersect Õε (1) earlier paths
which are longer than π; we just need to deal with the case
where π intersects many short paths added earlier. Here is the
key idea: Suppose that π intersects more than c · O(log n)
short paths, for some number c > 1. Each of these short
paths is a path between some canonical pair in a region above
R, meaning that each short path has one endpoint on some
external separator of R. As there are only O(log n) external
separators of R, pigeonhole principle implies that c of these
short paths all touch the same external separator path, which

of R.

of the edges of G into O(n/r) subgraphs called regions,
such that each region R (1) has at most r vertices and (2)
shares at most s boundary vertices
